fig8_1: Two side-by-side panels. The left panel plots the one-dimensional Poisson solution on the interval from minus one to one: open circles for the Chebyshev numerical values at N equals sixteen sit exactly on the solid exact-solution curve, which dips and rises in a smooth wave. The right panel is a semilog plot of maximum error versus N, with the error axis logarithmic; the markers fall along a straight descending line, reaching machine precision near ten to the power minus sixteen by N equals twenty-four, demonstrating exponential spectral convergence.
tbl8_1: Table listing maximum error against polynomial degree N for the one-dimensional Poisson problem, showing the error dropping roughly two orders of magnitude per increment of two in N until it flattens at machine precision, about two point two times ten to the power minus sixteen, by N equals twenty-four.
fig8_2: Two side-by-side panels. The left panel overlays two solution curves on the interval from minus one to one: the variable-coefficient case with coefficient one plus x squared has visibly smaller amplitude than the constant-coefficient case, the suppression being strongest near the boundaries where the coefficient is largest. The right panel verifies the constant-coefficient computation against its exact solution, with the numerical markers lying on the exact curve.
fig8_3: Two side-by-side panels. The left panel shows the mixed boundary-condition solution rising from zero at the left Dirichlet boundary at x equals minus one to a maximum at the right boundary x equals one, where the curve flattens to zero slope reflecting the insulated Neumann condition. The right panel is a semilog convergence plot of maximum error versus N; the error falls spectrally to roughly ten to the power minus fourteen by N equals sixteen, then plateaus as round-off from the large derivative-matrix boundary entries limits further gains.
tbl8_2: Table of maximum error versus N for the mixed Dirichlet-Neumann problem, showing spectral decay that levels off near ten to the power minus fourteen, a slightly higher noise floor than the pure Dirichlet case because the boundary entries of the first-derivative matrix grow as order N squared and amplify round-off.
fig8_4: Two side-by-side panels for the nonlinear Bratu equation with lambda equal to one half. The left panel shows the symmetric bell-shaped solution computed for several values of N, the curves overlapping to confirm convergence. The right panel is a semilog convergence-history plot of residual or correction norm versus iteration number: Newton iteration drops almost vertically in five to eight steps showing quadratic convergence, while fixed-point iteration declines along a gentle straight line showing slow linear convergence.
fig8_5: A grid of six panels, each showing one computed eigenmode of the Laplacian for N equals thirty-six, plotted on the interval from minus one to one and annotated with its points per wavelength and eigenvalue error. The low modes with high points per wavelength are smooth sinusoids resolved to near machine precision, while higher modes approaching pi, about three point one four, points per wavelength become visibly distorted as accuracy collapses, illustrating the fundamental resolution limit.
tbl8_3: Table comparing exact and numerical eigenvalues for N equals thirty-six with their points per wavelength and absolute and relative errors, showing near machine precision for modes above pi points per wavelength and an abrupt collapse of accuracy at mode twenty-three, where points per wavelength reaches about pi.
fig8_6: A scatter plot of the Chebyshev tensor-product collocation grid on the square from minus one to one for N equals sixteen. The points form a grid that is dense near all four edges and corners and sparse in the interior, the clustering toward the boundaries supplying the resolution that gives spectral accuracy in two dimensions.
fig8_7: Two side-by-side panels for the two-dimensional Poisson problem at N equals sixteen. The left panel is a three-dimensional surface of the solution, a single smooth hump rising from the flat zero boundary. The right panel is a contour plot of the same solution with the clustered Chebyshev grid points overlaid; the maximum error is about ten to the power minus twelve.
fig8_8: A sparsity, or spy, plot of the two-dimensional Laplacian matrix for N equals sixteen, an array of size N minus one squared by N minus one squared. Nonzero entries appear as dots forming a regular block-banded pattern: dense diagonal blocks from one Kronecker term and scattered diagonal stripes from the other, the structure arising from the Kronecker product construction.
tbl8_4: Table of sparsity statistics for the two-dimensional Laplacian across increasing N, reporting matrix size, nonzero count, percentage density, and nonzeros per row, showing density falling roughly as one over N while nonzeros per row grow linearly, far denser than the fixed five-point finite-difference stencil, the cost of spectral convergence.
fig8_9: Four panels in a two-by-two grid for the Helmholtz equation at wavenumber k equals seven, near resonance with the two-four eigenmode at about k equals seven point zero two. Panel a is a three-dimensional surface of the solution showing oscillatory wave-like structure. Panel b is a contour plot with the localized Gaussian forcing centre marked. Panel c is a semilog plot of solution amplitude at the forcing centre as k sweeps from three to twelve, spiking sharply at the two-four eigenvalue marked by a coral dashed line and at other Dirichlet eigenvalues marked by faint grey lines. Panel d shows the two-four Dirichlet eigenmode itself; its contours match those of panel b, revealing that the near-resonant solution locks onto the eigenmode pattern.
fig8_10: Two side-by-side panels for the quantum harmonic oscillator. The left panel overlays the first five eigenfunctions on the interval from minus eight to eight: Chebyshev numerical values shown as dots sit on the solid exact Hermite-function curves, the wavefunctions oscillating in the centre and decaying to zero at the edges. The right panel is a semilog convergence plot of eigenvalue error versus N for the lowest two eigenvalues, comparing the Fourier and Chebyshev methods; both descend exponentially to machine precision, but the Fourier curves reach it with noticeably fewer points.
tbl8_5: Table comparing Fourier and Chebyshev eigenvalue errors for the lowest two states of the quantum harmonic oscillator with domain half-width eight across increasing N, showing both methods reaching machine precision but the Fourier method converging faster for this problem.
